blocks.text: Chemical shift is an important parameter in NMR spectroscopy and represents the position of a signal relative to a reference compound. Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄ (commonly known as TMS) is used as the standard reference and its signal is assigned a value of 0.0 ppm. All other signals due to the hydrogen nuclei (protons) in the sample compounds are measured relative to this TMS zero point.

blocks.title: Chemical shift
blocks.text: The position of a peak in a ¹H NMR spectrum relative to TMS peak is called the chemical shift (δ) which is measured in parts per million (ppm) unit.
Chemical shift indicates the electronic environment of a proton. Protons in different environments have different δ values, while those lying in same environment have same δ value.

blocks.title: Did You Know?
blocks.text: TMS is particularly suitable as a standard compound for NMR because all 12 of its protons have the same chemical environment and produce a single sharp peak. Moreover, the protons on TMS appear at the extreme right region of the spectrum (due to the low electronegativity of silicon) and do not overlap with most organic proton signals. TMS is chemically inert and volatile, which makes it easy to remove after use.

blocks.alt: Structure of tetramethylsilane: a silicon atom in the centre bonded to four CH3 groups, above, below, left (H3C) and right. Label: Tetramethylsilane (TMS).
blocks.caption: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) (original drawing after the structure in the book's Did You Know box).

blocks.text: For example, in the ¹H NMR spectrum of methanol (Figure 30.2), the relative position of peak for methyl (-CH₃) hydrogens at 3.35 ppm compared to 0.0 ppm of TMS is the chemical shift of these protons. Similarly, O-H hydrogen of methanol has a chemical shift of 4.80 ppm.

blocks.alt: A 1H NMR spectrum on a delta scale from 6 to 0. A short peak at 4.80 (label in blue) and a tall peak at 3.35 (label in pink) stand on the baseline, and a peak labelled TMS stands at 0. Top left, the displayed formula of methanol with the three C-H hydrogens in pink and the O-H hydrogen in blue.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.2: 1H NMR Spectrum of Methanol (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 30.2).

blocks.text: Protons (¹H) in a molecule are surrounded by electrons and this electron density affects the appearance of an NMR spectrum. Protons in different parts of a molecule are in different "environments" because of the atoms and bonds near them.

blocks.title: Chemically equivalent protons
blocks.text: All the protons (¹H) found in chemically identical environments within a molecule are chemically equivalent, and they exhibit the same chemical shift in the ¹H NMR spectra of that molecule.

All the protons in TMS, methane, ethane, benzene and propanone (acetone) are chemically equivalent. Each of these compounds gives rise to a single absorption peak in its ¹H NMR spectrum (Figure 30.3).

blocks.alt: Displayed formulas of methane, ethane, benzene and cyclohexane. Every hydrogen atom in each molecule is labelled Ha.
blocks.caption: All the hydrogen atoms in these molecules have same chemical environment (original drawing after the structures printed in 30.3).

blocks.alt: A 1H NMR spectrum with a PPM scale from 3 to 0 and a single sharp peak near 0.2. Inside the plot, the displayed formula of methane and the words: The protons are equivalent and give one NMR signal.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.3: 1H NMR spectrum of methane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 30.3).

blocks.text: On the other hand, a molecule which has sets of protons that are chemically different from one another, have different chemical shift and give rise to more than one peaks.

blocks.alt: Two boxes. First box: propane, with the six end hydrogens labelled Ha and the two middle hydrogens Hb, and methanol, with the three C-H hydrogens Hb and the O-H hydrogen Ha; text: Molecules having two different chemical environments for protons. Second box: 1-chloropropane (Hc, Hb, Ha from the chlorine end) and ethanol (CH3 hydrogens Hc, CH2 hydrogens Hb, O-H hydrogen Ha); text: Molecules having three different chemical environments for protons.
blocks.caption: Molecules having two and three different chemical environments for protons (original drawing after the boxes printed in 30.3).

blocks.text: For example, a proton on a -CH₃ group is different from the one on -CH₂- and O-H in ethanol (C₂H₅OH) molecule. Similarly, all the three protons of -CH₃ have same environment, while the two protons of -CH₂- have same environment. The chemical shift of a proton (¹H) is affected by the electron density of its surrounding chemical environment. Protons surrounded by high electron density (alkyl groups) have lower chemical shift values, whereas protons surrounded by a low electron density (near electronegative atoms like F, O, N, Cl etc.) appear at high chemical shift values. For example, methyl (-CH₃) protons in the ¹H NMR spectrum of methanol appear at 3.35 ppm due to a higher electron density around them as compared to O-H proton, which appears at 4.80 ppm due to the presence of electronegative oxygen next to it (Figure: 30.2).

A ¹H NMR spectrum has a chemical shift (δ) range of 0 – 12 ppm. The chemical shifts for different environments of protons have been given in Table 30.1. This data table is helpful in identifying and predicting the environment of protons in ¹H NMR spectrum of an unknown compound.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The name ‘1,1,2,2-dichloroethane’ is not possible: four locants (1,1,2,2) need four chlorine atoms, i.e. 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane, Cl₂CH–CHCl₂. If 1,2-dichloroethane, ClCH₂–CH₂Cl, was meant, the answer is the same: all its protons are equivalent and there is one environment.
